title: The 10 Most Important Teaching & Learning Studies of the Last 50 Years
author: Busch, Bradley
summary: Bradley Busch of InnerDrive counts down ten studies he argues have most shaped modern classroom practice, moving chronologically from Miller's 1956 working-memory research through to Chen's 2017 metacognition study. Along the way he covers Rosenthal and Jacobson's 1966 study on teacher expectations, the Stanford marshmallow studies on delayed gratification, Mueller and Dweck's growth-mindset research, Hattie and Timperley's model of effective feedback, Dunlosky's 2013 ranking of study techniques, Thornton's research on mobile phones and concentration, a modern replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve, Fletcher and Sarkar's three-part model of resilience, and Chen's metacognition study. For several entries he draws out a specific classroom implication rather than just summarizing the finding, for instance using Dunlosky's ranking to specifically warn against relying on summarisation, highlighting, and re-reading as primary study techniques. The piece closes by framing this fifty-year run as evidence of real cumulative progress in educational psychology, while acknowledging that findings like the Thornton phone study haven't been fully replicated.
points: Busch uses Dunlosky's 2013 synthesis to draw a sharp practical line: retrieval practice and spaced practice are the highest-utility study strategies, while highlighting, re-reading, and keyword mnemonics are explicitly "not recommended as primary learning tools."
He extracts Hattie and Timperley's three-question feedback model as the practical takeaway from their research, rather than just citing the paper's existence.

His summary of the marshmallow research draws the causal-sounding conclusion that early delayed gratification predicted a range of adult outcomes, while treating the underlying finding about self-control as the throughline.

He flags that the Murre and Dros replication of Ebbinghaus's forgetting curve found a counterintuitive twist, a next-morning memory boost attributable to sleep, that complicates the popular "forgetting curve" story.
quotes: He found that roughly seven items could be recalled in normal adults, give or take two. While this number has since been re-investigated, this finding ultimately proved the limited capacity of working memory.
This shows that when teachers have high expectations, they subconsciously alter their behaviours to be more supportive, allowing student achievement to be maximised.

Retrieval Practice and Spacing emerged as the most effective techniques, benefiting learners of all ages and abilities, and consistently enhancing performance across different tasks and educational settings.
On the other hand, techniques such as summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonic, imagery and re-reading ranked lowest in terms of utility and are not recommended as primary learning tools.

An intriguing discovery emerged: after 24 hours of learning, participants experienced a memory boost, remembering more on the morning of the second day than on the night of the first. This improvement was due to the negative impact of fatigue on memory and the restorative power of sleep.
